pr_comments: Triage: It looks like this is super messy. Closing for now. We can approach this again later.

issue_context.title: Set the AuthenticationResult via a new feature on the HttpContext
issue_context.body:
Today the authentication middleware resolved the `AuthenticateResult` for the current request/endpoint and stores the Principal on the HttpContext but doesn't store the other properties (Ticket, or AuthenticationProperties). Getting at these requires another call to AuthenticateAsync with the right scheme which can be a pain to get at. We should make this available via a feature on the HttpContext

cc @Tratcher @HaoK
comments: Could this be the result be extended out to give people that feature they want to return reasons from policies?
We could do something similar for the authz middleware, but what would it be, like the result of the last authorization failure?

Well you know there have been lots of requests for this sort of thing, including allowing information on why a policy failed, which mixes authn and authz in a way we don't like, but if this could be used it might make a lot of people happy.
This isn't likely to be what you are looking for as it really only maps to the default authenticate call we do in the auth middleware
Is this servers? Feels more like security. Moving it for now.
Reopening as this is something SignalR would like to have.

Idea (courtesy Chris): Using a DIM, we can add the Ticket to the `IHttpAuthenticationFeature`, then if the User is set by someone else the Ticket could be nulled out so we don't have inconsistency with the two values, and we would remap the User to the Ticket.User.

Thanks for contacting us.

We're moving this issue to the `Next sprint planning` milestone for future evaluation / consideration. We would like to keep this around to collect more feedback, which can help us with prioritizing this work. We will re-evaluate this issue, during our next planning meeting(s). 
If we later determine, that the issue has no community involvement, or it's very rare and low-impact issue, we will close it - so that the team can focus on more important and high impact issues.
To learn more about what to expect next and how this issue will be handled you can read more about our triage process [here](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/master/docs/TriageProcess.md).
@BrennanConroy As part of the signalr PR can you address this as well?
We'll need to rethink this change. Adding `AuthenticationTicket` to the `IHttpAuthenticationFeature` creates a circular reference between Http.Features and Authentication.Abstractions.

Looking through the code, would adding a new feature (`IAuthenticateResultFeature`) after https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/52eff90fbcfca39b7eb58baad597df6a99a542b0/src/Security/Authorization/Policy/src/AuthorizationMiddleware.cs#L70 work?

You still have the issue of the ticket being out of sync with the User. How about adding the new feature, but implement it with a class that also implements IHttpAuthenticationFeature and does the user re-mapping?

Set it here instead of setting the User:
https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/52eff90fbcfca39b7eb58baad597df6a99a542b0/src/Security/Authorization/Policy/src/PolicyEvaluator.cs#L52-L53
Why set it there and not right outside that call? Someone could replace the `IPolicyEvaluator`, so doing the work regardless of the implementation of that interface would be better.
Only to be consistent about assigning User vs Ticket. I don't know if anyone calls the IPolicyEvaluator outside of the middleware.
Well its was intended so if you wanted to be able to mimic 'normal auth', you could use the policy evaluator, so I guess it should have the same semantics as setting the User today ideally

review_comments: I have a project that has multiple authentication scheme and no default scheme. So I don't even have `UseAuthentication` in the pipeline. Is it possible that the AuthenticateResult/Ticket/Properties for other scheme be available in this feature. If so I think this feature should be also set in Authorization middleware.

You should consider create a virtual scheme that aggregates the multiple schemes (implements authenticate by calling authenticate on all the schemes and merges them), then could just use that as your default scheme
There should be an extension method added to retrieve the new data. Users shouldn't need to directly access features for common operations. `HttpContext.GetAuthResult()`

So is this really better than just having them call context.AuthenticateAsync(), that usually is equivalent to this.  But we could add a sugar method that uses this feature called context.GetDefaultAuthenticateResult() I guess which is just a cache on top of our cached result that you'd normally get back from AuthenticateAsync...
Yeah, the value add here is pretty suspect. The end user experience is about the same. @davidfowl

I should share why I wanted this. In SignalR the HttpContext sometimes goes away (long polling) but we want to get the user and authentication result so we can do expiry checks and abort the connection if the auth ticket expires.

Okay so for that situation, its mostly about getting access to the default authentication the middleware did, since you can't even call Authenticate again if you wanted...

Does it seem reasonable to only target the no HttpContext case for this feature then?  Since if you have httpContext, just call AuthenticateAsync() to get the default result.  Maybe we call this DefaultAuthenticateResultFeature, and then it maps exactly to capturing the AuthMiddleware's result and nothing more.  It doesn't need to have any interaction with HttpContext at all?
I'd expect you'd still want to set it in the MVC and SignalR auth filters, those update the user based on the current authz policy don't they?
Yeah but that doesn't really work, you can combine a User out of the ClaimsPrincipals, but there's a reason we don't preserve the meta data there, since which one would you put in there.

Then this preserved result data is misleading if it's not going to match the HttpContext.User in MVC or SignalR.

Alternatively, make this a `List<AuthenticationResult>` so you can preserve all of them.

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/b879e587370fc669a3433e89c5311423e6bb1ee1/src/Security/Authorization/Policy/src/PolicyEvaluator.cs#L40-L44
As an optimization, we should implement this feature in the servers as well. It's usually a file that needs to be updated.
That mainly works if you're setting a property on an existing feature, not assigning a new feature.
Why can't this check for the feature?
Should maybe name this something a little less crappy...  DefaultAuthenticateResultFeature since it maps to DefaultAuthenticate?

@davidfowl the AuthenticateResult is partially redundant with User and creates a Source-of-truth/consistency problem. What ensures User and the AuthResult stay in sync? Nothing.

There's a few ways to address this:
A) Do we actually need the whole AuthResult? Maybe we only need to add the AuthProperties and/or error? Those could be added to the existing IHttpAuthenticationFeature using default interface properties.
B) Obsolete IHttpAuthenticationFeature.User in favor of IAuthenticationResultFeature. Have HttpContext.User use the new feature.
C) Have IAuthenticationResultFeature derive from IHttpAuthenticationFeature and have User defer to Result.Principal.

I suggest A.
A) sounds good. Lets add the AuthenticationProperties, Ticket, Error, what else?

This is two separate things though isn't it?  HttpContext.User is mutable, while this is effectively just exposing the result of AuthenticateAsync(DefaultScheme) as it occurred from the Auth middleware.  It's effectively read only and not a mechanism for modifying the effective user for the request.
Hence why I was suggesting we name this something more like IDefaultAuthenticateResultFeature

Well the result is able to represent None(no auth info) and Failed(error), we could always just store the User inside the result object if we want it to be consistent, so context.User is setting the underlying results object's user?

It's super weird that we'll have two effective users on the request. Developers will not know what to do with that.

Ticket is redundant also, it's just Principal + Properties.
@HaoK thoughts?

Well I'm just saying something like this:
Context.User // just alias for Context.Authentication.Result.Ticket.Principal
Context.AuthenticateResult // lets you get access to the full result
So then they can also check `Context.AuthenticateResult.None`/`Context.AuthenticateResult.Failure`
I don't think we should have AuthenticateResult as a first class property on the HttpContext
